newsitem.title: USA: U.S. asks waiver of Georgian diplomat's immunity.
newsitem.headline: U.S. asks waiver of Georgian diplomat's immunity.

text.p: The State Department said on Thursday it had formally asked Georgia to waive the diplomatic immunity of a Georgian diplomat involved in a five-car crash in central Washington in which a teen-age girl was killed.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters the Georgian ambassador was called to the State Department on Thursday afternoon where he was also asked to ensure that the diplomat, Gueorgui Makharadze, not leave the country until a decision had been taken on the waiver.

Burns said Secretary of State Warren Christopher was personally concerned over the incident, which prompted an outcry in Washington over the issue of diplomatic immunity. Christopher was writing to Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze on Thursday night to back up the U.S. requests.

In the letter, Burns said Christopher would reaffirm the request "that Georgia lift (Makharadze's) diplomatic immunity so that he might face trial here in the United States and that he might not leave the United States until we get an answer from the Georgian government." Christopher would also say he was "concerned by the direction the case is heading."
Burns said Georgian ambassador Tedo Djaparidze had given no response to the the U.S. request on Thursday but Washington hoped to have a formal answer from Tbilisi on Friday.

The request for a waiver of immunity was unusually being lodged before receipt of the formal police investigation report, Burns said. Makharadze, 35, could face charges ranging from negligent homicide to second degree murder if tried by a U.S. court.
